english: A polyhedron can never be bent ?!
topic: Short notes: a remark on curve closure, whether polyhedra can be bent, a Hurwitz extremal problem on polygons, a plan to treat the rotation of a fluid-filled body with Klein's parameters, a question on force fields with only closed orbits (Darboux–Halphen), and the start of a statement on expanding continuous functions in series of rational integral functions.

triage.modern_statement: The note asks whether every closed polyhedral surface in R^3 is rigid. Here the faces are rigid plates joined by hinges along the edges. 'Bent' means a continuous non-trivial motion, other than a rigid motion of the whole body, that keeps every face congruent to itself. This is the classical 'rigidity conjecture' for polyhedra. Cauchy (1813) proved it for convex polyhedra. Bricard (1897) found flexible octahedra, but they intersect themselves. That left the question open for embedded non-convex polyhedra.
triage.answered_by: Partly settled before the note: Cauchy (1813) showed convex polyhedra are rigid, and Bricard (1897) gave self-intersecting flexible octahedra. Gluck (1975) showed that 'almost all' simply connected closed polyhedra are rigid. Robert Connelly settled the general question in the negative in 'A counterexample to the rigidity conjecture for polyhedra', Publ. Math. IHÉS 47 (1977), 333–338. Klaus Steffen later found a 9-vertex flexible polyhedron. Follow-up: Connelly, Sabitov and Walz proved the Bellows conjecture (1997) that the volume stays constant while a polyhedron flexes. Sabitov had a related proof in 1995, which comes from background knowledge and was not confirmed in the searches.

evidence.claim: Cauchy proved that every convex polyhedron is rigid, meaning it cannot move while keeping the shape of its faces. Gluck showed that 'almost all' simply connected polyhedra are rigid.
The Bricard octahedra are non-convex, self-crossing flexible polyhedra.

It had long been believed that all non-self-intersecting closed polyhedra with rigid faces and hinged edges are rigid (the 'Rigidity Conjecture'). Connelly found the first counterexample in 1977, and Steffen soon gave a 9-vertex flexible polyhedron.
Reference: R. Connelly, 'A counterexample to the rigidity conjecture for polyhedra', Publ. Math. IHÉS 47 (1977), 333–338.
The Bellows conjecture (a flexible polyhedron keeps a constant volume while it flexes) was proved by Connelly, Sabitov and Walz, Beiträge zur Algebra und Geometrie 38 (1997).

triage.why: 'Polyeder kann nie verbogen werden ?!' matches the classical Cauchy/Bricard question of whether polyhedra are rigid or can flex. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Cauchy settled the convex case and Bricard gave self-intersecting flexible examples. Connelly's embedded flexible polyhedron of 1977 shows the general claim 'never' is false. The field is still active, as shown by recent work such as Gallet–Grasegger–Legerský–Schicho on Bricard octahedra and studies of flexible polyhedra in spaces of constant curvature. The note itself is undated, so I can't say whether Hilbert wrote it before or after Bricard's 1897 paper. My reading of what he meant by 'bent' (verbogen) is inferred from the wording.
